analogy.p: Imagine a satnav screen that records how far you are from home each minute. If the line on the screen rises steeply, you are covering ground quickly, like a motorway; if it rises gently, you are in a town; if it flattens, you have stopped for petrol; and if it falls, you are driving back home. The slope of the line is your speed. A curve is like pressing the accelerator and watching the slope get steeper. The analogy breaks down because a real satnav shows the route as a map, whereas a distance-time graph only records how far you are along a straight line, not the turns you take.
analogy.t: A road trip on a satnav map

bullets: The x-axis is **time (s)** and the y-axis is **distance (m)**; always label both axes with quantity and unit.
At any time on the x-axis, go straight up to the line and across to the y-axis to read the **distance at that time**.
The graph describes motion in a **straight line** only; it tells you nothing about the shape of the path.
The graph starts at the origin (0,0) if the object starts at the start line at time zero, but it can start higher up if the object starts some distance away.
A line that goes **up** means the object is **moving away** from the starting point; a line that goes **down** means it is **coming back** towards it.
A **horizontal** line means distance is not changing, so the object is **stationary** (at rest).

Strictly, the distance an object has travelled can never decrease, so a graph with a downward section is plotting the **distance from the start** (position), not the total distance travelled. Exam questions draw it this way and mark it as 'returning to the start'.
core.p: A **distance-time graph** plots **time on the horizontal (x) axis** and **distance on the vertical (y) axis**. Each point tells you how far the object has gone (or how far it is from its starting point) at that moment. Time always goes on the x-axis because time is the thing that changes by itself; distance is what we measure as a result. Reading the graph is really reading a story: when does the object move, how fast, when does it stop and does it come back?

bullets: **gradient = change in distance / change in time = speed** (m/s).
**Steeper line = faster** speed; **shallower line = slower** speed.
**Horizontal line: gradient = 0**, so speed = 0; the object is at rest.
**Straight sloping line: constant gradient**, so **constant speed** (zero acceleration).
**Curved line: the gradient is changing**, so the speed is changing, which means the object is **accelerating** (or decelerating).
A straight line does not have to start at zero: only its steepness matters when finding speed.
The equation to recall is **distance travelled (m) = speed (m/s) x time (s)**, rearranged to speed = distance / time and time = distance / speed.
Link: on a velocity-time graph the gradient is the acceleration, so do not mix up which graph you have; the y-axis label tells you.
core.p: The most important idea is that **the gradient (slope) of a distance-time graph equals the speed**. Gradient is defined as change in y divided by change in x, which here is change in distance divided by change in time. That is exactly the definition of speed: **speed = distance / time**. So the steeper the line, the more distance is covered every second, and the faster the object is moving. This is why a graph can replace a table of numbers: the shape tells you the speed directly.

bullets: Step 1: pick **two points on a straight section**, as far apart as the section allows and where the line crosses grid intersections.
Step 2: read the **change in distance** (y2 - y1) and the **change in time** (x2 - x1).
Step 3: **speed = change in distance / change in time**.
Step 4: write the answer with the correct **unit (m/s)**.
Example: a line from (0 s, 0 m) to (8 s, 40 m) has speed 40 / 8 = **5 m/s**.
If the graph uses minutes or km, convert first: 12 km in 30 minutes is 12 000 m in 1800 s = 6.7 m/s (to 2 s.f.), or keep as 24 km/h if the question allows.
Do **not** just read one value from the y-axis and divide by one value on the x-axis for a line that does not start at zero; use the **changes**.
Check the answer is sensible against typical speeds (a cyclist at 60 m/s would be wrong).
core.h: Calculating speed from a straight section: the method
core.p: To find the speed from a straight section you draw a **gradient triangle**: a right-angled triangle whose sloping side is the line. The vertical side is the **change in distance** and the horizontal side is the **change in time**. Always choose points far apart, because reading a small triangle magnifies reading errors, and choose points that sit exactly on grid lines so the readings are accurate. Examiners give a mark for showing the numbers you used, so write the sum out.

bullets: **Straight line upwards:** moving away from the start at a **constant speed** equal to the gradient.
**Horizontal line:** **stationary**; the distance stays the same for that time interval.
**Straight line downwards:** moving **back towards the start** at constant speed (the size of the gradient is the speed; the negative sign shows direction).
**Curve getting steeper:** the object is **speeding up** (accelerating).
**Curve getting shallower (flattening out):** the object is **slowing down** (decelerating).
**Vertical line:** impossible, because it would mean covering a distance in zero time (infinite speed).
**Line going back to the x-axis at zero distance:** the object has returned to its starting point.
Say 'between 8 s and 12 s' not 'in the middle part' so the marker can see exactly where you mean.
core.p: Exam questions often say 'describe the motion shown by the graph'. The model approach is to go through the graph **section by section**, saying what the object is doing, **quoting the speed or the distance and times** from the graph. Using the word 'constant' for straight lines and 'stationary' for horizontal lines earns the marks. Always say in which direction the object is moving relative to the start if the line goes down.

bullets: A **tangent** touches the curve at **one point only** and has the same steepness as the curve at that point.
Place a ruler on the point so that the curve is equally above and below the ruler on each side of the point (the 'balance' method), then draw a long line.
Draw a **large** gradient triangle on the tangent (not on the curve) using points far apart.
**Speed at that time = gradient of the tangent = change in distance / change in time.**
For the curve d = t squared, at t = 5 s the tangent passes through (3.5 s, 10 m) and (6.5 s, 40 m), so speed = 30 / 3 = **10 m/s**.
The **average speed** over the first 5 s is 25 / 5 = 5 m/s, which is different from the speed at 5 s; **average speed uses a chord (whole interval), instantaneous speed uses a tangent**.
A steeper tangent later on shows the object is **accelerating**; you can compare tangents at two times to see the change in speed.
Marks are usually given for: tangent drawn correctly, triangle shown or two points read, correct calculation, and an answer within an accepted range because of drawing tolerance.
core.h: Curved graphs and tangents: the speed at an instant
core.p: When the line is curved, the speed is different at every moment, so there is no single gradient triangle. To find the speed at **one particular time** you draw a **tangent**: a straight line that **just touches the curve at that point and does not cut across it**, with the curve's direction matching the line at the touching point. You then find the gradient of that tangent. The gradient of the tangent is the speed at that instant. This is a Higher tier skill that you must practise with a ruler.

bullets: **average speed = total distance / total time.**
Include the time for rests; they count towards total time.
In the journey figure (5 m/s out for 8 s, rest 4 s, 5 m/s back for 8 s) the total distance travelled is 40 + 40 = 80 m in 20 s, so average speed = **4 m/s**.
The final distance from the start is 0 m, but the average speed is not zero: speed is about distance travelled, **velocity** is about displacement.
The average **velocity** for that return trip is 0 m/s because the overall displacement is zero.
A diagonal line joining the start and end points of any journey has a gradient equal to the average speed (or average velocity if the graph is of displacement).
If a question gives a table instead of a graph, plot the points first or work out distance and time differences directly.
core.h: Average speed for a whole journey
core.p: The speed from a gradient is the speed for that section only. If the question asks for the **average speed for the whole journey**, you use the **total distance travelled divided by the total time taken**, including any time spent stationary. Stopping lowers the average speed, which is why a cyclist who rests has a lower average than their moving speed. Make sure you add up **total distance** (if the object turns round, the total distance is the sum of all sections, not the final distance from the start).

bullets: **Scalar:** magnitude only (distance, speed, time, mass). **Vector:** magnitude and direction (displacement, velocity, force, acceleration).
Gradient of a **distance-time** graph = **speed**; gradient of a **displacement-time** graph = **velocity**.
A negative gradient on a position graph means velocity is in the **negative direction** (back towards start).
An object moving round a circle at constant speed has a constant speed but a changing velocity because its direction keeps changing.
The word 'speed' in the question tells you to give a size only; the word 'velocity' tells you to include a direction.
The area under a distance-time graph has **no useful meaning** at GCSE; do not use it.
Link to Newton's laws: a constant speed in a straight line (straight sloping d-t line) means the resultant force is zero.
core.h: Speed, velocity, distance and displacement on these graphs
core.p: Distance is a **scalar** (size only) and displacement is a **vector** (size and direction). Speed is a scalar and velocity is a vector. A distance-time graph strictly gives speed, because distance has no direction. But when a graph shows the position of an object from a starting point and the line goes down, the gradient is negative, and then it is really a **displacement-time graph** whose gradient is **velocity**. For GCSE you can use the same method, and you can say 'negative gradient means moving in the opposite direction'.

bullets: **Walking: about 1.5 m/s.**
**Running: about 3 m/s.**
**Cycling: about 6 m/s.**
**Car: about 25 m/s** (about 56 mph, in a 60 mph limit it is up to about 27 m/s).
**Train: about 55 m/s** (high-speed lines).
**Aeroplane: about 250 m/s.**
**Speed of sound in air: about 330 m/s** (values around 340 m/s are also accepted).
**Wind speed** varies a lot, from a few m/s in a breeze to more than 30 m/s in a storm.
Use these to estimate how long a journey takes: a 1500 m walk at 1.5 m/s takes 1000 s, about 17 minutes.
core.p: The specification expects you to know **typical values** for everyday speeds so that you can check whether an answer is sensible and make estimates. These are approximate and used for comparison. Memorising them also helps you spot calculation slips such as a person walking at 150 m/s.

bullets: **Steeper line = higher speed**; compare gradients, not where the lines end.
**Crossing point = same distance at the same time**: read the time and the distance.
Parallel lines have the **same gradient**, so the same speed; they never meet.
A line that starts higher is **ahead** at time zero (a head start).
Example figure: A moves away from X at 4 m/s; B starts 60 m from X moving towards X at 2 m/s. They meet when 4t = 60 - 2t, so **t = 10 s** at **40 m** from X.
To find who finishes first in a race, find which line reaches the finish distance at the **smaller time**.
When a faster object catches a slower one, its line crosses the slower line from below.
core.h: Comparing two objects on the same graph
core.p: Putting two lines on one set of axes lets you compare them. The **steeper** line is the faster object. If the lines **cross**, the two objects are at the **same position at the same time**, so they meet (or one overtakes the other). Where one line starts higher up, that object started further from the reference point. A downward line towards an upward line shows two objects approaching each other.

bullets: Time on the **x-axis**, distance on the **y-axis**; **scale must be linear** and use more than half the grid.
Plot each point with a small cross or dot; accuracy to within **half a small square**.
Straight sections joined with a **ruler**; stationary sections drawn as a horizontal line.
Convert a described section: 'cycles at 5 m/s for 20 s' adds **100 m** to the distance.
Start the next section from where the last one ended; the graph is **continuous** (no jumps).
A line of best fit is only used for experimental data with scatter; journey graphs go through the points.
Check the final distance and time against the information given in the question.
core.h: Drawing a distance-time graph from data
core.p: You may be given a table or a description and asked to **draw the graph**. Choose scales so the graph fills most of the grid, use sensible even steps (1, 2, 5 or 10 per square), label axes with units, plot points accurately to within half a square, and join them with a ruler for straight sections (or a smooth curve for accelerating motion). For a described journey, work out the end point of each section using distance = speed x time before plotting.

bullets: Use a **metre rule** or tape for distances; mark start and finish lines clearly.
A stopwatch has a human **reaction time** error of about 0.2 s; light gates and a data logger remove this.
Repeat each timing at least three times and calculate a **mean** to reduce random error.
Use longer distances so that the reaction-time error is a smaller percentage of the total time.
Plot distance against time; the **gradient of the line of best fit** gives the average speed.
If the trolley speeds up on a slope, the graph is a curve and you need tangents to find speed at a point.
Control variables: same surface, same slope, same mass of trolley.
Safety: stop moving objects safely (a box or a sandbag at the end of the track).
core.h: Practical link: measuring speed in the lab
core.p: You can collect data for a distance-time graph by timing a trolley, ball or student over marked distances, or using light gates and data loggers. A graph of distance against time is drawn and the gradient gives the speed. Using more repeats and a clear method reduces **random errors**, while choosing a start and end line carefully reduces **systematic** error. Light gates are more accurate than stopwatch timing because they remove human **reaction time**.

bullets: Work out what **one small square** is worth on each axis before reading anything.
Read values at **eye level** to the line, and use a ruler to carry values across.
Show units in every step of a calculation line.
When asked for a time when a given distance is reached, go **across** from the distance and **down** to the time.
To find the **total time stationary**, add up the lengths of all horizontal sections.
If you are asked for the speed in km/h, convert: **1 m/s = 3.6 km/h**.
Check your answer is in the range of typical speeds.
If the graph goes off the grid, extend the line with a ruler only if the question allows.
core.h: Common graph skills and data handling
core.p: Graph questions test skills as well as knowledge. You may need to read a value between gridlines, convert units, work out the scale on each axis (the scales on the x and y axes may be different), or find the time at which a certain distance is reached. Take care when each small square represents an unusual amount, such as 0.5 s or 4 m. Writing the scale of each axis on your paper before you start prevents slips.

bullets: **d-t gradient = speed**; **v-t gradient = acceleration**; **v-t area = distance**.
A straight sloping d-t line corresponds to a **horizontal** v-t line (constant speed).
A curved, steepening d-t line corresponds to a **sloping straight** v-t line (constant acceleration).
**Newton's first law:** constant speed in a straight line (or at rest) means the forces are balanced.
**Newton's second law:** a curved d-t graph shows acceleration, so there is a resultant force.
**Terminal velocity:** the d-t graph becomes a **straight line** once speed is constant.
Exam phrases: 'the gradient is the speed', 'the line is horizontal so the object is stationary', 'the object is accelerating because the gradient is increasing'.
core.h: Links to other topics and exam-board phrases
core.p: Distance-time graphs link to the velocity-time graph, to Newton's first and second laws, to terminal velocity and to stopping distance. A change in the gradient of a d-t graph means acceleration, which requires a **resultant force**. Knowing how d-t and v-t graphs relate lets you swap between them, which is a typical 'challenge' question. AQA mark schemes use phrases such as 'constant speed', 'stationary', 'gradient' and 'accelerating'.

exam: **Command words:** 'describe' = say what happens in each section with numbers from the graph; 'calculate' = show the working; 'explain' = give a reason using the gradient or forces; 'compare' = use comparative words (faster, steeper) for both.
**1 mark:** reading one value from a graph (give units) or stating that a horizontal line means stationary.
**2 marks:** calculating a speed: 1 mark for change in distance / change in time with correct values, 1 mark for the answer with units (e.g. 40 / 8 = 5 m/s).
**3 marks:** a tangent question: tangent drawn touching the curve, gradient triangle with values, answer within the accepted tolerance.
**4 marks:** 'describe the motion': mention each stage with speeds or distances: moving away at constant speed, stationary, returning, with times.
**6 marks (extended):** combine the graph with the equation and with forces: e.g. link a curved section to acceleration and a resultant force in the direction of motion, with calculations.
**Model phrases:** 'the gradient of the line is the speed', 'the line is horizontal so the object is stationary', 'the gradient is increasing so the object is accelerating'.
Always **show your triangle** on the graph and write the numbers you read; a wrong answer with correct working still gains method marks.
Check the **scale** on both axes before reading anything; small squares may not be 1 unit.
Use a **ruler and sharp pencil** for tangents; the mark scheme usually has a tolerance range for the gradient.
If a question gives you the average speed and the time, use distance = speed x time to find the endpoints, then you can draw or check the graph.
Finish by checking your answer against typical speeds (walking 1.5 m/s, cycling 6 m/s, car 25 m/s).

mistakes.r: A horizontal line on a distance-time graph means the object is stationary (gradient = 0); constant speed is a straight sloping line.
mistakes.w: A horizontal line means the object is moving at constant speed.

mistakes.r: Use the change in distance divided by the change in time (the gradient) from two points on the line.
mistakes.w: Speed = distance read from the y-axis divided by time read from the x-axis, even when the line does not start at zero.

mistakes.r: A line going down on a distance-time graph means the object is moving back towards the start; a curve that flattens means it is slowing down.
mistakes.w: A curve downwards means the object is slowing down.

mistakes.r: The graph shows distance against time, not the shape of the path; say moving away from or towards the start.
mistakes.w: The object is going downhill / uphill when the line slopes.

mistakes.r: A tangent touches the curve at only one point with the same gradient as the curve at that point; draw it with a ruler and a big triangle.
mistakes.w: Drawing the tangent so it cuts across the curve or using a chord.

mistakes.r: The unit of speed is metres per second (m/s); include it in the final answer.
mistakes.w: Giving the speed with no units, or in m instead of m/s.

mistakes.r: Convert distances and times to consistent units (m and s) before calculating, unless the answer is asked in km/h.
mistakes.w: Mixing units, such as km on the graph and seconds in the calculation.

mistakes.r: The area under a distance-time graph has no meaning at GCSE; area is used on velocity-time graphs.
mistakes.w: Using the area under a distance-time graph to find something.

mistakes.r: Average speed = total distance travelled / total time, including time stationary.
mistakes.w: Average speed for a journey is the final distance divided by time, or the mean of the section speeds.

mistakes.r: A steeper line means a higher speed; the distance travelled is shown by the height reached.
mistakes.w: Steeper line means the object travelled further.

summary: The specification asks you to draw and interpret distance-time graphs for an object moving in a straight line, to calculate speed from the gradient of the graph, and (for an accelerating object) to find the speed at a particular time by drawing a tangent and measuring its gradient. It also expects you to know typical speeds and to link graphs to the speed = distance / time equation. It matters because graph questions appear in almost every Paper 2 and are a reliable source of 3 to 6 marks.

terms.d: How far an object moves, a scalar quantity measured in metres (m), with no direction.
Includes both the distance and direction in a straight line from the start to the finish point; a vector quantity.
How fast an object is moving, a scalar quantity; distance travelled per unit time, in metres per second (m/s).
Speed in a given direction; a vector quantity.
A quantity that has magnitude (size) only.
A quantity that has magnitude and an associated direction.
The steepness of a line, equal to the change in the y-axis value divided by the change in the x-axis value.
Not moving; a horizontal line on a distance-time graph.
Equal distances travelled in equal time intervals; a straight sloping line on a distance-time graph.
A straight line drawn to touch a curve at one point, with the same gradient as the curve at that point.
Total distance travelled divided by total time taken.
The rate of change of velocity, measured in m/s2; shown by a curved distance-time graph.
A right-angled triangle drawn on a graph to measure the change in y and the change in x for a gradient calculation.
The time between a stimulus and a person responding to it, usually about 0.2 s, which causes error in stopwatch timing.
A sensor that records the time a beam of light is broken, used to measure speed more accurately than a stopwatch.
Motion along a straight path, which is the only type of motion a GCSE distance-time graph describes.

worked.ans: (a) 1.5 m/s and 3.0 m/s (0 m/s while waiting). (b) Average speed = 270 / 160 = 1.7 m/s (to 2 s.f.).
worked.q: A student walks to school. In the first 60 s she travels 90 m. She then waits at a crossing for 40 s. In the next 60 s she travels 180 m. (a) Calculate her speed in each moving section. (b) Calculate her average speed for the whole journey. [5 marks]
steps: Section 1: speed = distance / time = 90 / 60 = 1.5 m/s (1 mark).
Average speed = 270 / 160 = 1.6875 m/s (1 mark for correct answer rounded).

worked.ans: Speed at 5.0 s = 10 m/s; average speed over the first 5.0 s = 5.0 m/s.
worked.q: The distance-time graph of a car accelerating from rest follows d = t squared (d in m, t in s). A tangent drawn at t = 5.0 s passes through (3.5 s, 10 m) and (6.5 s, 40 m). Calculate the speed of the car at 5.0 s and compare it with its average speed over the first 5.0 s. [4 marks]
steps: Tangent gradient = change in distance / change in time (1 mark).
Average speed over the first 5 s = 25 / 5.0 = 5.0 m/s, so the speed at 5 s is double the average, because the car has been speeding up throughout (1 mark).

worked.ans: From 0 to 8 s the object moves away from the start at a constant speed of 5 m/s, reaching 40 m. From 8 to 12 s it is stationary (the distance stays at 40 m). From 12 to 20 s it moves back towards the start at a constant speed of 5 m/s and arrives back at its starting position at 20 s.
worked.q: Describe the motion shown by a graph in which the line rises from (0 s, 0 m) to (8 s, 40 m), is horizontal until 12 s, then falls to (20 s, 0 m). [4 marks]
steps: Identify each section and quote values.
Section 2: horizontal means stationary for 4 s.
Section 3: negative gradient, back to the start at 40 / 8 = 5 m/s.
